source.title: Steering Large Language Model Activations in Sparse Spaces
source.authors: Reza Bayat; Ali Rahimi-Kalahroudi; Mohammad Pezeshki; A. P. Sarath Chandar; Pascal Vincent

record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE-derived sparse features in Gemma-2 models and reports their steering effects and feature-overlap patterns. It uses a different method and setting from the toy-model superposition work.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition as background and cites the original toy-model work, but does not reproduce toy networks or test feature sparsity-versus-importance geometry. The relevant original results here are SAE feature extraction, sparsity scaling, and steering outcomes. The study also reports many behavioral and benchmark outcomes unrelated to the claim versions; they are not catalogued here.
record.test_reason: This is a steering-method paper. It uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool and reports its own SAS method's performance: steering shifts, open-ended judge scores, benchmark effects, compositionality, and the overlap and sparsity of its own SAS vectors. Superposition appears only as background motivation. No result measures whether real-model features are superposed or spread across neurons, or whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical. The fall in active SAS features with SAE width is a property of the paper's filtered steering vectors; calling it 'monosemanticity' is the authors' interpretation, not a test of V4 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that SAS enables precise, interpretable, compositional steering of Gemma-2. They say that scaling SAE width improves the sparsity ('monosemanticity') of SAS vectors, and that SAS does not degrade MMLU/TruthfulQA and can improve them at moderate lambda. They acknowledge SAE features are not guaranteed fully monosemantic at limited dictionary size.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained JumpReLU SAEs and contrastive prompt-pairing to derive sparse steering vectors, then intervenes in SAE activations of Gemma-2 models. It does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports outcome changes with SAE width, tau, lambda, layer, and prompting setup. It notes greater steering with lower tau and higher lambda, and that steering is most evident in intermediate layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Behaviour-specific SAS steering vectors contain fewer active SAE features as SAE width grows from 16K to 1M, especially at tau=0.9. Raw active features per input stay roughly stable (Fig 7, Figs 28-31).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastively selected behaviour feature sets become sparser with larger SAE dictionaries (behaviour representations concentrate on fewer latents at larger widths).

fits_no_version.finding: Steering vectors for different behaviours share SAE features. For example, positive refusal and negative hallucination share 30 features at 65K and 20 at 1M. Dense CAA vectors show cosine similarities up to |0.74|.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment-relevant behaviour directions share representational components in LLMs.

record.problems: The evidence concerns SAE-derived steering features rather than native model-feature geometry. Monosemanticity is inferred from sparsity and overlap measures rather than checked against ground-truth features. Many relevant values appear only in figures, and the text reports no uncertainty estimates. SAEs trained on base models are applied to instruction-tuned models.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports further behavior-specific overlap matrices in Appendix J (Figures 24–25), per-behavior scaling plots in Appendix K.1 (Figures 28–31), and many steering results across layers, behaviors, and hyperparameters. These were not included because they repeat the selected aggregate trends or would require many separate matrix-cell and plotted-condition rows; the retained rows cover the relevant scaling, steering, and overlap findings.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no test of whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity.
All: no measure of features spread across neurons, and no evaluation of SAE recovery of sparse features (SAEs are assumed to work).
All: no test of completeness, stability across seeds or widths, or canonicity of SAE features (no feature matching across widths).

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 and its V4/V5 labels are reclassified. The paper assumes superposition and SAE disentanglement as motivation and measures only its own method's vectors. The monosemanticity claim rests on sparsity counts of filtered steering vectors, with no interpretability or ground-truth check. SAEs were trained on base models and applied to instruction-tuned models.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Alternative causes of polysemantic neurons and whether polysemanticity alone evidences superposition.

The study uses SAE-derived features to extract and steer behavior-related representations, but does not measure how features are distributed across native neurons or establish that the SAE dictionary recovers all model features.
The study examines a monosemanticity proxy and feature overlap, but does not test feature completeness, stability across training or settings, or canonical status.
Whether model features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional subspaces.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Applied SAE-derived SAS vectors during inference and evaluated target-behavior answer probabilities on held-out multiple-choice examples.

conditions.value: AI coordination, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy, refusal

rows.measure: Change in probability of the behavior-matching answer
rows.baseline: Unmodified model (lambda = 0); probability change is measured relative to this baseline.
rows.value: Figure-only; the text says positive steering generally increases matching behavior and negative steering suppresses it.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the result, but the plotted values are not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: Measures SAS steering performance on behaviour multiple-choice probabilities, i.e. the study's own method. It does not test whether models contain sparse features an SAE recovers (V4).

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Varied SAE dictionary width and measured the number of active features in SAS vectors.
rows.measure: Number of active features in SAS vectors
rows.value: Figure-only; the text reports that increasing SAE width increases SAS-vector sparsity, particularly at tau = 0.9.
rows.note: The authors interpret the decrease in active SAS features as improved monosemanticity and disentanglement; exact plotted counts are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Counts active features in the method's filtered SAS vectors versus SAE width. This is a property of the steering vectors after tau filtering and shared-feature removal. It does not test SAE features' completeness, stability or canonicity (V5) or feature recovery (V4); 'monosemanticity' is the authors' label, with no ground-truth check.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Varied SAE dictionary width and measured active features in raw sparse activations before SAS filtering.

conditions.value: positive and negative completions before SAS filtering

rows.measure: Number of active features in raw SAE sparse activations
rows.value: Figure-only; the text reports that the total number of raw active features remains stable across SAE widths.
rows.note: The study reports a qualitative trend, not exact counts.
rows.check: Raw active-feature count stable across SAE widths is a descriptive SAE statistic used to interpret SAS sparsity. It does not bear on any version's effect.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated multiple-choice steering performance while scaling SAE width.
rows.measure: Behavior-matching answer probability under positive and negative steering
rows.value: Figure-only; the text reports stable positive-steering performance and minor degradation for negative steering at higher tau values.
rows.note: The authors note that lambda was fixed at ±1 and that sparser vectors may require stronger steering.
rows.check: Steering performance of the study's own method under SAE scaling. This is method evaluation, not a measure of superposition or dictionary-feature properties.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Counted shared SAE features between the positive refusal direction and negative hallucination direction.
rows.note: The paper describes this cross-over as feature overlap between positive refusal and negative hallucination directions.
rows.check: Value 30 is correctly read from Fig 24(d), refusal row by hallucination column. But overlap between two behaviours' steering vectors measures behavioural correlation, not whether SAE features are canonical units.

rows.subject: Gemma-2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Counted shared SAE features between the positive refusal direction and negative hallucination direction.
rows.note: The paper reports fewer shared features in the 1M SAE overall and describes increased sparsity and disentanglement.
rows.check: Value 20 is correctly read from Fig 25(d) at 1M width. It is the same behavioural-correlation measure of the method's vectors and does not bear on V5.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
